item.question: An adhesive brand has no product demonstration budget and no headline. What does the reproduced Fevicol execution do instead, and what does the device require of its audience?
item.answer: It carries the whole argument in one photograph: an overcrowded Indian suburban train with dozens of men hanging off the side of a carriage, on which a 'FEVICOL — The Ultimate Adhesive' panel is mounted. There is no headline and no body copy; the adhesion claim is made by the juxtaposition alone, and the viewer infers it rather than being told. What the device requires is that the scene already be culturally familiar — it recruits an everyday sight the audience knows, so it does not travel to an audience that has not seen an Indian suburban train. That dependence is the extractor's observation from the plate, not something the source states; the book's caption asserts only that good creative work is possible for a humble category.
item.support: Caption: 'The Fevicol campaign was proof that scintillating creative advertising can happen for even a humble adhesive.' Plate inspected at 566 px.
item.confounders: The source does not date this execution and gives no outcome data for it.

item.claim: Pandey states that Indian advertising has too few women leading agencies, accepts this as a failing of the industry's senior men including himself, and locates the problem specifically at retention rather than entry: competent women leave and their accumulated knowledge is lost. He states that the conflict between the two roles he describes must be resolved by the business rather than by the individual, and names extended maternity and paternity leave approvingly. He contrasts advertising with Indian banking, where he names several women running major banks.

source_terms: The Law of Credentials
The crucial ingredient in the success of any brand is its claim to authenticity.
Credentials are the collateral you put up to guarantee the performance of your brand.
item.claim: Law 6. The authors start from customer disbelief: prospects are suspicious and discount most product claims. They argue one claim takes precedence over all others because it makes the others credible — the claim to authenticity, to being the real thing. Benefit claims made without credentials are, on their account, generally ignored, because every competitor makes the same sort of claim; the same benefit claims attached to a credential carry much more weight. They extend the point to buyer behaviour generally with the empty-restaurant observation: people prefer to wait for a table where there is a queue rather than eat in an empty room.

mechanism.text: Credentials work as collateral. A claim about performance is unverifiable at the point of choice, so the prospect looks for something that stands behind it; where a brand supplies that, the prospect will believe almost anything else it says. Absent it, benefit claims fall into the undifferentiated mass that provokes "that's what they all say".

scope.conditions: wherever prospects cannot verify a product claim before buying

caveats.text: 'the crucial ingredient in the success of any brand' is a universal claim demonstrated by one advertising line (Coca-Cola's 'the real thing') and two consulting cases of the authors' own
the Act and Datastream cases are the authors' own client work, reported by them with the outcome figures they chose to report and no independent source

source_stated_problems: many companies run branding programs almost devoid of credentials
an endless parade of almost meaningless benefits . . . they each lack credibility so they are generally ignored
source_stated_remedies: when the benefits are structured around some aspect of a brand's credentials, they carry much more weight

positive.description: Act positioned as 'the largest-selling contact software', with the credential carried on every surface including the box

intra_source_relations.note: leadership is the credential the authors reach for first
credentials are what makes a brand usable to reporters

an asterisk suggests the claim it's attached to is not true
Happy White Mom with Shopping Bags
item.claim: Sullivan identifies a family of signals whose presence is itself the tell. A package promising "made with real cheese" or "contains real fruit" invites the inference that something is not real, and he gives the reductio: nobody sells a phone by saying it is made with real phone. An asterisk on a price, he argues, can legitimately be read as the sentence saying "we're lying", because it announces that a briefcase of qualifications is propping the number up. Stock photography is his third case — the manufactured handshake, the executive staring thoughtfully into a screen — which he says reeks of inauthenticity, and he names the most-demanded stock image in his own count of the genre. His stated underlying principle, taken from Frank Rose, is that authenticity is scarce and value tracks scarcity.

mechanism.text: Each signal is a defensive move that would be unnecessary if the claim were secure, so a reader who has learned the pattern treats the defence as a symptom. Sullivan grounds the learned pattern historically: the collapse of institutional authority since Watergate has produced a population of eye-rollers and sceptics who no longer accept "because we said so", so signals that once passed are now inspected.

scope.conditions: consumer advertising addressed to an audience the source characterises as habitually sceptical; his historical account is specifically American

caveats.text: the causal history — Watergate, then a chain of fallen icons, therefore scepticism about advertising — is a sweeping cultural narrative offered without evidence, and is specific to the United States
the asterisk reading is a rhetorical move, not a claim about how most readers actually process fine print; the source does not claim to have tested it

the source's own remedy, authenticity, is not defined in a way that could be checked on a finished piece; he borrows a two-part split (brand authenticity and audience authenticity) from another author rather than supplying a test

source_stated_problems: more advertisers decided to simply replace their bullhorns with bullshit
if those products were authentically cheese or fruit, would they feel the need to say those things?
inauthentic brand messaging leads to doubt, while inauthentic audience exchange leads to ridicule and backlash
source_stated_remedies: promote a message that honestly reflects the truth about a brand, and express it in a way that doesn't come across as bullshit to customers
admitting your commercial is a paid message with an agenda is one effective way to disarm distrust
embrace the suck: take an obvious weakness and use it to accentuate the product's main strength

positive.description: Domino's 'Pizza Turnaround', which opened by replaying focus-group video of customers saying the pizza was bad before stating the brand would fix it; and Buckley's cough syrup comparing its own taste to public-restroom puddle water under the line 'It tastes awful. It works.'

counter.description: a truck advertisement carrying an asterisked monthly payment; and the stock-photography genre the source lists by type

intra_source_relations.note: the exclamation point is one instance of the pattern
corporate voice is the same failure at the level of register

provenance.section: Authority gets replaced with fake; To thine own brand, be true; Embracing the suck. (spine 13)

item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Attention"; Google for Business resources, section "A – Attention"; Think with Google, section "A = Attention: Hook the viewer"
item.question: The source's Attention principle asks for two distinct things. What are they, and what means does it name for achieving them?
item.answer: Hooking attention and sustaining it — "Hook and sustain attention with an immersive story" — so an arresting opening that then loses the viewer does not satisfy the principle. source_terms: Pacing can be understood as a kind of cadence or “timing” a viewer will apprehend from one part to another, as well as the degree of dynamism or activity they perceive.
ordering is about function; pacing is about feeling
item.claim: Rhythmic pacing from part to part within a sequence-based format is a powerful way of keeping a grid's use lively. Pacing is the cadence or timing a viewer apprehends from one part to the next, and the degree of dynamism they perceive. Varying it from slow to fast or quiet to dynamic does two things: each new page or screen engages the reader afresh, and the reader is cued to a significant change of content, which clarifies informational function. Pacing is distinct from ordering, which accounts for the location and actual sequence of raw content; pacing is the formal variation imposed on that. Ordering is about function; pacing is about feeling. Applying the system's rules for sizes, weights and styles will automatically create a recognisable rhythm supporting the informational ordering, but that intrinsic pacing may seem too even for the designer's concept, and it falls to the designer to balance deriving pacing from the content's own ordering against invigorating the viewer.

mechanism.text: A change in formal treatment is read as a change in kind, so varying the rhythm signals a content boundary without any explicit marker.

item.question: What is the objection to 'the Indian middle class' as a planning input, and why is the author's own position in the story evidentially interesting?
item.answer: That the category has no agreed definition, so its size varies enormously with whichever definition is chosen, and a number quoted without its definition is therefore uninterpretable — yet it is routinely used as a planning input, with capacity built against it. The objection is methodological rather than empirical: she is not arguing the middle class is smaller than claimed, but that 'how big is it' is not a well-formed question until the definition and the population base are stated. WHAT MAKES HER POSITION EVIDENTIALLY INTERESTING is that she discloses her own role in creating the myth she now attacks — she was part of the industry that produced and circulated the number. That is testimony against interest, which is why the record treats the disclosure as STRENGTHENING the object rather than as a caveat on it: an insider naming a construction she helped build is a more reliable witness to how it was built than an outside critic. The affluence-layer material she offers instead was recovered from Table 5.1 in this pass, which exists only as an image in this copy: income percentiles, household counts and per-tier ownership of colour TV, refrigerator, two-wheeler, car, landline, washing machine and PC, sourced to IRS 2008.
item.support: Ch. 5; and the author's own account of her role in the middle-class myth.
item.confounders: The lesson is not 'the middle class is a myth' but 'a segment label without a stated definition and population base is not a planning input'. The first is a claim about India; the second is a rule about labels.

source_terms: The scooter carries with it an aura of safety (over its macho cousin, the motorcycle) that its engineering does not quite merit. Its smaller wheelsize actually makes it a less stable vehicle than the motorcycle but the air of safety that it so convincingly carried had more to do with images that surrounded it.
item.claim: Desai argues that the Bajaj scooter carried a convincing aura of safety that its engineering does not merit — its smaller wheels make it less stable than the motorcycle it was felt to be safer than — and that the perception came from the images surrounding it: the stepney, the space for a whole family, the dickey for the household's sundries. The perceived attribute is produced by what the object is seen to enable, not by the property it names.
item.interpretation_basis: The engineering claim about wheel size is stated as fact but is not sourced. The argument that the safety perception derives from surrounding imagery rather than from stability is the author's interpretation.

mechanism.text: An attribute term is attached to whatever most visibly stands for it. Where the visible evidence for "safe" is a vehicle that carries a family and their belongings responsibly, the term attaches there, and the physical property the term literally names goes unconsulted.

scope.conditions: India, the decades in which the scooter preceded the motorcycle in middle-class ownership. The author writes retrospectively, after the motorcycle had displaced it.

caveats.text: the stability claim is asserted, not sourced; smaller wheels do affect stability but the source cites no engineering authority
no measurement of perceived safety is offered; the perception is asserted from the author's memory of the object's standing
the same essay offers a second and stronger reading of the object (sk_dmpl_0031); they are two readings, not a logical relation

source_stated_problems: a perceived product attribute can be produced by surrounding imagery and contradict the physical property it names
